reader.counterexample: A page prints "passed" because the title of a saved result says so, and nothing recomputes the verdict from the data underneath.
reader.does_not_prove: A passing check limits what a claim may say; it does not make the claim true outside what that checker examined.

example.text: A replay reads a test file that declares a monitor caught an agent scheming, recomputes the verdict from the recorded trace, and rejects the run when the declared verdict does not follow from that trace.

reader.governs: When a stated result may be used as evidence at all.
reader.plain: A result counts only when an independent check can reproduce it from the inputs it came from. A confident statement on its own counts for nothing.
reader.potential_misread: That a checked result is certain, when the check only limits how much the result can claim.
reader.refuses: Treating a written label as if it were the true result.
reader.requires: The inputs the claim was computed from, a certificate of how it was derived, and a checker that recomputes the verdict and accepts it.
reader.why_it_matters: Answers such as "a model said so" or "the record is labelled passed" carry no weight until something independent works the answer out again.

reader.does_not_prove: A checker accepting one certificate shows only that this certificate passed this checker, and says nothing about the producer's other output or about bugs in the checker itself.

example.text: The certificate kernel lab keeps the code that emits certificates separate from a small checker that decides them. A companion Lean example is compiled by the real Lean verifier, whose kernel rejects an invalid proof whatever the producer intended.

reader.governs: Which part decides a claim: the small checker, never the producer.
reader.plain: A claim is trusted only when a small, separate check works it out again from the evidence supplied with it. The program that produced an answer never approves its own answer, however capable it is.
reader.potential_misread: That a powerful, confident producer can vouch for its own output, so the small separate check can be skipped when the output looks authoritative.
reader.refuses: Trusting the producer in place of the checker.
reader.requires: A small checker that decides by reading a certificate, kept separate from the program that produced it.
reader.why_it_matters: The part someone has to audit stays small and fixed while the programs generating answers grow larger and faster.

reader.governs: Whether a given caller may cause a given effect, decided separately for each effect when it is requested.

reader.governs: When a cached or reused result may stand in for a fresh computation.
reader.plain: A stored result can be reused only when the exact inputs it was built from are unchanged; a matching name or location is not enough. If the inputs changed it must be rebuilt, and if they cannot be found there is no result.
reader.potential_misread: That a matching name or file name makes it safe to reuse a stored result, so checking the inputs again is wasted effort.
reader.refuses: Reusing a cached result by name after its inputs have changed.
reader.requires: A declared list of inputs, an identity computed as a hash of those inputs, and a hash comparison that decides between reuse and recompute.
reader.why_it_matters: A stale or tampered result cannot pass as fresh just because its name or path matched.

reader.governs: What status missing evidence gets, and in which direction a status may change between stages.
reader.plain: Something built from parts is only as trusted as its weakest required part. A part with no evidence counts as blocked, and a later step can lower trust but never quietly raise it.
reader.potential_misread: That enough passing parts can outweigh a blocked one, when the weakest required part sets the status of the whole.
reader.refuses: Passing something by default when no check ran.

reader.why_it_matters: A missing check is treated as a reason to stop, so a release that finds private material or overclaiming wording stops instead of shipping.

reader.governs: Whether an absence of evidence may count as a negative result, and within what scope.
reader.plain: Finding no evidence for something differs from showing it is false. You can call an absence a "no" only inside a list you have checked completely; otherwise the honest answer is "unknown".

reader.refuses: Treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence.

reader.why_it_matters: "We did not see a problem" stays separate from "there is no problem", which is how unnoticed failures get signed off.

reader.governs: What a calculation may return when the conditions it needs do not hold.
reader.plain: A calculation may return a number only when the conditions it needs actually hold. When they don't, it hands back a labelled refusal naming the reason, never a quiet number or blank that the next step reads as an answer.
reader.potential_misread: That a number coming out at the end means the conditions were met, so a value can be used without checking that the calculation had what it needed.
reader.refuses: Returning a number or a NaN when the conditions for computing it were never checked.
reader.requires: A declared precondition for returning a value, and a labelled refusal with a reason and evidence on every other path, including missing libraries and undefined values.
reader.why_it_matters: A missing input or an out-of-range condition shows up as a visible gap, instead of a plausible figure that a later page prints as a real result.

analogy.text: A bank transfer completes only if the bank can reverse it or has marked it final. A transfer in several legs goes ahead only while the starting balance is unchanged and no other transfer is touching the same account.

reader.counterexample: A step writes to a shared path and is counted as complete because the call returned, with no check of the starting state and no single-writer rule, so two writers interleave and the result matches neither.
reader.does_not_prove: Only the named paths reject a changed starting state or a second writer, and the registry records that linking these failure cases to the full rule is still unchecked.

example.text: The mission transaction work spine completes a change in several steps only when the starting state it expected is still the current one, so a run whose starting state was replaced in the meantime fails with a parent-mismatch error instead of overwriting the newer state.

reader.governs: When a change to stored state may be counted as complete.
reader.plain: A change only counts as done if there is a stated way to undo it, or a clear note that it can never be undone. A change in several steps goes ahead only if its expected starting point is unchanged and nobody else is changing the same thing.
reader.potential_misread: That every change must be reversible, when a change may also be declared permanent so long as it says which it is.
reader.refuses: An irreversible write made without these checks.
reader.requires: An undo step or a declared point of no return, and for changes in several steps, a check that the expected starting state is still current plus a rule that only one writer works on a path at a time.
reader.why_it_matters: A half-finished change cannot be counted as complete, which is how a system ends up in a state nobody chose and nobody can reverse.

analogy.boundary: A dated reading only tells you when it was correct; whether it is still correct today needs a fresh reading.

maps.analogy: a number describing ongoing electricity use
maps.doctrine: a statement about something that keeps changing

maps.analogy: the figure shown on the meter
maps.doctrine: the value stated

maps.analogy: the date the reading was recorded
maps.doctrine: the time the value was taken

maps.analogy: which meter the reading came from
maps.doctrine: the source the value was read from

maps.analogy: the procedure for taking a fresh reading
maps.doctrine: the rule for reading the value again

analogy.text: An electricity meter reading is useful on a bill only if it records the date, which meter it came from and how to take a fresh reading. The bare number says nothing about today's usage.

reader.counterexample: A page prints a running total once and leaves it up for weeks with no date and no way to recompute it, so an old reading looks like a live figure.
reader.does_not_prove: Flagging undated numbers does not make any dated number current or correct, and the rule for refreshing this axiom's own figures has not been written yet.

example.text: The fact-claim audit flags any changing number that carries no date or refresh rule with a fixed error code, so a live count cannot be published as current without saying when it was taken and how to recompute it.

reader.governs: When a value read from a changing system may still be stated as current.
reader.plain: A number about something that keeps changing is a reading taken at one moment. To be usable later it has to say when it was read, where it was read from and how to read it again.
reader.potential_misread: That attaching a date and source makes a number current, when they only make it possible to check.
reader.refuses: A count from a changing system stated with no date and no way to refresh it.
reader.requires: A value with the time it was taken, its source and a rule for reading it again, refreshed or withdrawn once the source has changed.
reader.why_it_matters: A number that was true once is not read weeks later as if it were still true, after the thing it measured has changed.

analogy.text: A customs declaration clears goods only when it passes the form check, comes with its supporting paperwork and states what it does not vouch for. A convincing letter describing the shipment clears nothing.

reader.counterexample: A persuasive standard written in prose is treated as binding because it sounds authoritative, though no parser accepted its structure and it lists no evidence requirements or limits.
reader.does_not_prove: A document that passes the parser is well formed; whether its content is complete or correct is a separate question.

example.text: The executable doctrine grammar component accepts a standard only when its structure parses and its evidence requirements and limits statement are present, and rejects a standard written in prose that claims authority without that structure.

reader.governs: Whether a rule document may govern, or is only something to read.
reader.plain: A rule can govern only when it passes a fixed format check and lists the evidence it must produce and what it leaves out. A well-written paragraph on its own is something to read.
reader.potential_misread: That passing the format check means the rule fully covers its subject, when the check looks only at the rule's structure.
reader.refuses: Prose claiming the force of an executable rule.
reader.requires: Acceptance by the grammar parser, a list of the evidence the rule must produce and a declared statement of what it does not cover.
reader.why_it_matters: A confident paragraph is not enforced as a rule just because it sounds authoritative.

nodes.plain: Treat a fixture label, a declared verdict, a route status, a count or a line of public copy as a statement to check. Recompute the verdict from the lower-level evidence, and keep a negative fixture with a deliberately wrong label, so that a check which only repeats labels fails.

analogy.boundary: The marking picture covers recomputation and the planted wrong answer only; a real check may read many more kinds of evidence than one exam paper.

maps.analogy: the exam paper itself, worked from scratch
maps.doctrine: the evidence underneath the verdict

maps.analogy: working the answer out again instead of copying the key
maps.doctrine: recomputing the verdict from the evidence

maps.analogy: the planted wrong answer the marking must catch
maps.doctrine: the negative test case the checker must reject

analogy.text: A teacher marks an exam by working each answer out from scratch instead of copying the answer key, and slips in a paper with a planted wrong answer to confirm the marking catches it.

reader.counterexample: A summary copies a component's self-reported "passed" onto a status board without recomputing it and without any test case that could fail.
reader.does_not_prove: Recomputing one verdict shows that this verdict follows from its evidence, and says nothing about verdicts nobody recomputed.

example.text: The benchmark-integrity replay recomputes a score from the recorded run instead of trusting the reported number, and keeps known gaming attempts as test cases that the replay must catch.

reader.governs: Whether a stated result may be used as evidence.
reader.plain: Trust a result only after working it out again from the underlying evidence, and keep a deliberately wrong test case that the check has to reject.
reader.potential_misread: That checking a result once makes it safe for good, when the check only covers that result against that test.
reader.refuses: Repeating a declared verdict, label or count as if it had been checked.
reader.requires: Recomputing the verdict from lower-level evidence, and a negative test case that the checker rejects.
reader.why_it_matters: It stops a label saying 'passed' from being copied from report to report when nobody has worked out whether it was true.

nodes.plain: A claim may say no more than the named checker, validator, registry or witness route actually computes. If the checker decides only a local contract, describe the result as that local contract and nothing wider.

analogy.boundary: The blood test covers one measurement only; it leaves out how several checks combine, where the overall result is as weak as the weakest of them.

maps.analogy: the iron test only supports a statement about iron
maps.doctrine: the claim's strength is limited to what the named check decides

maps.analogy: writing 'perfectly healthy' after one narrow blood test
maps.doctrine: wording that reaches past the check to the whole system

analogy.text: A blood test for iron tells you about iron levels. It gives you no grounds to write 'in perfect health' on the chart.

reader.counterexample: A component checks that a result record has the expected fields, and a summary page treats that field check as evidence that the underlying property holds everywhere.
reader.does_not_prove: Capping a claim at what its checker computes does nothing to make a weak checker stronger.

example.text: The formal-math readiness gate computes how far its available evidence reaches and reports only that much, so a local check is never written up as overall readiness.

reader.governs: How strong a claim may be, given the check that accepted it.
reader.plain: A statement can only be as strong as the exact thing the check settled. If a check confirms one small, local fact, the writing around it must stay at that size.
reader.potential_misread: That because the underlying check was real, any confident sentence built on it is also safe, when the sentence can only claim what the check decided.
reader.refuses: Using a checker that decides one local contract to support wording about the whole system.
reader.requires: Limiting each claim to what its named checker, validator, registry or witness route actually computes, with the limit computed from the underlying obligations.
reader.why_it_matters: It keeps a narrow, real check from being written up as a broad claim, so readers can see what was actually tested.

nodes.plain: Let a small verifier, parser, harness, compiler route, registry contract or kernel decide what is trusted, in place of a broad written account of why a result looks right. The code that produces results may be large; the code that decides should be small enough for a person to read and rerun.

analogy.boundary: The weighing plate covers only who decides and why the shopper is kept out; a simple checker can still make mistakes of its own.

maps.analogy: the weighing plate that checks each item again
maps.doctrine: the small checker that rereads and decides

maps.analogy: the shopper, who cannot confirm their own bag
maps.doctrine: the large producer kept out of the decision

analogy.text: At a self-checkout, the weighing plate weighs each item again to confirm what was scanned. The shopper packing the bag never gets to declare the bag correct.

reader.counterexample: A large model is trusted because it sounds sure of its answer, and no separate checker rereads anything, so the producer is also the judge.
reader.does_not_prove: A small checker is easier to audit, and it can still be wrong.

example.text: The certificate kernel lab keeps producers and the checker apart. A producer writes certificate material and a small kernel rereads it and decides, so the deciding code is the part you can read and rerun.

reader.governs: Where trust sits, between a large producer and the small checker that decides.
reader.plain: Put your trust in one small, simple step that redoes the work and decides. The large, complicated program that produced the answer stays out of that decision, because the thing being judged should not judge itself.
reader.potential_misread: That a capable, confident producer can vouch for its own output, when once the producer decides, no independent check is left.
reader.refuses: Accepting a large producer's own confidence in place of a small check that someone can read and rerun.
reader.requires: A small checker that rereads a certificate and accepts or rejects it, with the producer outside the decision.
reader.why_it_matters: The part you have to audit and rerun stays small, even when the systems producing answers grow large and hard to inspect.

kernel decide what is trusted, in place of a broad written account of why a

nodes.title: Concentrate trust in small checkers

nodes.plain: Permission to change something comes from the referenced proof, policy, result record and rollback evidence, each opened and checked, together with the current state of the repository. A credential, a role name, administrator wording or a phrase such as "trusted session" is never enough on its own to authorize a change.

analogy.boundary: The bank picture covers only the gap between holding a credential and being cleared to act; it leaves out the specific permissions, rules and side-effect records weighed at decision time.

maps.analogy: simply having the card number
maps.doctrine: a standing credential or role name, which carries no permission alone

maps.analogy: the bank deciding each payment against this account, now
maps.doctrine: permission worked out for each action from policy and current state

analogy.text: Knowing someone's card number does not move money. For each payment the bank checks this card, this amount and the current account before it lets the transfer through.

reader.counterexample: A change goes ahead because the caller holds a valid admin credential, and nothing checks that credential against the specific effect, the policy or the current state.
reader.does_not_prove: These components show how permission is worked out for the effects they handle, and say nothing about effects that never pass through them.

example.text: The tool-authority replay ties each tool effect to a declared scope and approval and rejects a scope that is too broad or a side effect nobody approved, so a tool being callable gives it no extra reach.

reader.governs: Whether an effect or change may go ahead.
reader.plain: Holding a credential, having a role name or being in a 'trusted' session gives no permission to change anything by itself. Permission is worked out again for each action, from the rules and the current situation.
reader.potential_misread: That a valid credential is enough to act, when the credential is one input and the change still has to be cleared for that exact action against the current state.
reader.refuses: Treating a standing credential, role name, admin wording, trusted session or an available tool as permission on its own.
reader.requires: Authorization worked out from looked-up proof, policy and current state, with each tool effect limited to its declared identity, scope, approval and side-effect records.
reader.why_it_matters: A component holding broad power cannot be talked into using it for someone else, because each action needs its own permission.
